voiced: Your vocal cords buzz while you make it. Put a finger on your throat: "zzz" buzzes, "sss" doesn't.
voiceless: No buzz from the vocal cords, just air. Compare "sss" (voiceless) with "zzz" (voiced).
aspirated: Followed by a puff of air, like the p in English "pin". Hold a tissue in front of your mouth and it moves.
unaspirated: No puff of air afterwards, like the p in English "spin".
no aspiration: No puff of air afterwards, like the p in English "spin".
bilabial: Made with both lips, like p, b and m.
labiodental: Bottom lip against the top teeth, like f and v.
dental: Tongue tip touches the back of the top front teeth.
alveolar: Tongue tip on the gum ridge just behind the top teeth, where English t, d, s and n are made.
postalveolar: Just behind the gum ridge, where English "sh" and the s in "measure" are made.
alveolo-palatal: Tongue tip down behind the lower teeth while the middle of the tongue rises toward the hard palate. Like "sh" said with a smile.
retroflex: Tongue tip curled up and back toward the roof of the mouth.
palatal: Middle of the tongue against the hard palate, the bony roof of your mouth. English y in "yes" is made here.
velar: Back of the tongue against the soft palate, where English k and g are made.
uvular: Back of the tongue against the uvula, the little flap hanging at the very back of your mouth.
pharyngeal: Made by squeezing the throat (the pharynx), below the mouth and above the voice box.
pharyngealised: A second, extra squeeze: while making the main sound, the back of the tongue pulls toward the throat, giving a dark, heavy colour.
glottal: Made in the voice box itself, by closing or narrowing the vocal cords. English h is glottal.
stop: Air is blocked completely, then released in a little burst. English p, t, k, b, d, g are stops.
fricative: Air is squeezed through a narrow gap, making a hiss or buzz. English f, s, sh, v, z are fricatives.
affricate: A stop that releases straight into a fricative, like English "ch" (t + sh) and "j" (d + zh).
approximant: The speech organs come close but not close enough to hiss. Smooth and vowel-like, like English y, w and r.
trill: The tongue tip (or uvula) vibrates several times in the airstream, like a rolled r.
tap: One very quick flick of the tongue, like the tt in American "butter".
nasal: Air goes out through the nose, like m, n and the ng in "sing".
sibilant: A hissing or hushing sound with strong, high-pitched friction, like s, z, sh.
syllabic: A consonant that acts as the vowel of its syllable, carrying the beat on its own.
close: Jaw nearly shut and tongue high in the mouth, as in "ee" and "oo".
close-mid: Tongue a little lower than for close vowels, as in Spanish e and o.
mid: Tongue halfway between high and low, like the relaxed "uh" in "about".
open: Jaw open and tongue low, as in "ah".
front: The highest part of the tongue is toward the front of the mouth, as in "ee".
central: The tongue is bunched in the middle of the mouth, neither forward nor back.
back: The tongue is pulled toward the back of the mouth, as in "oo".
rounded: Lips pushed into a round shape, as in "oo".
unrounded: Lips relaxed or spread, not rounded, as in "ee".
vowel: A sound where air flows freely, with no blockage. Vowels are described by tongue height, tongue position and lip shape.
